list.listitem: Neutropenia is classified as mild (ANC >1000-1500/μL), moderate (ANC 500-1000/μL), or severe (ANC <500/μL). C
Acquired neutropenia is more common than congenital neutropenia, with common causes being drugs and viral infections. C
Fever, cellulitis, stomatitis, gingivitis, abscess, sinusitis and pneumonia are commonly associated with neutropenia. C

If ANC is <1000/μL consider obtaining a blood smear, Coombs test, immunoglobulins, viral serology and cultures, antigranulocytes antibodies. If persistent, consider bone marrow aspirate. If ANC <500/μL and the patient is symptomatic, consider hospitalization. See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation. C

background.definition: Leukopenia refers to a white blood cell count less than 4000, and it may include neutropenia and lymphopenia. Neutropenia is defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <1500/μL in non-Hispanic whites and <1200/μL in African-Americans. Neutropenia may be classified as mild (ANC >1000-1500/μL), moderate (ANC 500-1000/μL), or severe (ANC <500/μL). Lymphopenia may be defined as < 1500/μL and severe lymphopenia as < 1000/μL.

list.listitem: Based on a large study of 25,222 participants, the prevalence of ANC <1500/μL is 4.5% in African-Americans, 0.79% in Caucasians, and 0.38% in Mexican-Americans.
The prevalence of ANC <1000/μL is 0.57% in African-Americans, 0.11% in Caucasians, and 0.08% in Mexican-Americans.

A study of over 32,000 adults identified relative lymphopenia in 20% (< 1000/μL) and severe lymphopenia (< 1000/μL) in 3%. The risk of all-cause mortality was increased in both groups, with a hazard ratio of 1.3 for relative lymphopenia and 1.8 for severe lymphopenia even after adjusting for a range of risk factors. The risk was greater in patients with an elevated inflammatory marker (CRP) and an increased red cell distribution width.
See the differential diagnosis table for common causes of acquired neutropenia, congenital neutropenia, and for rare causes of congenital neutropenia.
There are 4 main pathophysiologies for neutropenia: decreased production, increased destruction, sequestration, hypersensitivity reaction.
Decreased production may be due to viral infections, bone marrow failure or replacement, and chemotherapy.
Hypersensitivity reaction may be seen in association with drugs (see ).
Bone marrow replacement occurs with malignancy.
Sequestration occurs in hypersplenism
Increased destruction is seen in infections (see ) and with autoantibodies.
Screening for leukopenia by ordering a regular or annual WBC count is not recommended. C

Authors of an Australian study recommended screening for neutropenia in infants born to mothers with hypertension. Out of 249 infants 7.6% were neutropenic and 4.1% were both neutropenic and thrombocytopenic. However, there is no evidence that detection by screening improved any clinical outcomes.B

list.listitem: Elements of the history important in patients with neutropenia include fever,chills and recurrent mouth sores; fatigue; past history of leukemia, lymphoma, or aplastic anemia; family history of neutropenia; and cyclical neutropenia. It is also important to ask about medications that may cause leukpenia (see ).
Physical signs like fever >101°F, cellulitis, stomatitis, abscess, gingivitis, perirectal inflammation, colitis, sinusitis, and septicemia are also associated with neutropenia.
Pneumonia, both bacterial and fungal, can be a complication of neutropenia.
Traditionally, digital rectal exam is not recommended in neutropenic patients due to the potential risk of infection. However, this has not been substantiated by well designed clinical trials.

Initial evaluation includes a white blood cell (WBC) count with differential and calculation of the absolute neutrophil count (ANC). ANC can be calculated as a combined percentage of neutrophils and bands (if present) times the actual white cell count. For example, if 20% neutrophils and 2% bands, and the WBC is 4000 cells/μL, then the ANC is 22% x 4000 = 880 cells/μL.
If you suspect cyclic neutropenia, consider WBC 2 to 3 times/week for 4 to 6 weeks to confirm.
No additional testing is generally needed for ANC of 1000 to 1500/μL unless history and physical exam dictates.

If ANC is <1000/μL consider blood smear and the following specific tests: Coombs test to rule out hemolytic anemia and immunoglobulins rule out dysgammaglobulinemia, viral serology and cultures to rule out infections, and antigranulocyte antibodies to rule out autoimmune neutropenia.
Consider urine culture, chest x-ray and lumbar puncture in a febrile patient with ANC <500/μL.
If persistent neutropenia or pancytopenia, consider bone marrow aspiration/biopsy.

Procalcitonin, interleukin 6, and C-reactive protein are potentially useful biomarkers for evaluation of children with febrile neutropenia, but there is significant heterogeneity in the literature. In two studies of hospitalized children receiving chemotherapy with febrile neutropenia, serial procalcitonin levels predicted bacteremia and gram negative bacteria, but not severe sepsis.

In a series of 1888 persons 0 to 21 years presenting with an isolated ANC <1000 cells/mcl (no underlying risk factors, no previous neutropenia, normal platelet and hemoglobin, no immunodeficiency or malignancy or other serious comorbidity) the overall risk of serious bacterial infection was 2.4% based on positive cultures. Those without fever had a 0.4% likelihood, vs 6.2% if febrile.
In patients with cancer and febrile neutropenia, a clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of complications or death.
See algorithm in .
Assess patients with neutropenia with a thorough history and physical exam.

If moderate (ANC 500-1000/μL) or severe (ANC <500/μL), conduct diagnostic testing based on the history and physical findings and presentation. Recommended tests include a blood smear, Coombs test, immunoglobulins, viral serology and blood cultures, and antigranulocyte antibodies.
If mild neutropenia, repeat or perform serial CBCs every 3 to 4 weeks.
If cyclical neutropenia is suspected, consider more frequent WBC counts (2-3 per week for 4-6 weeks).
